evidenceRecords.text: The Royal Navy Type 45 Destroyers appear to have received a new C-UAS system for self protection against drones.
Images released recently by the UK MoD show HMS Dauntless (D33) sporting two mystery containers that are likely acting as interceptor drone launchers.
The Ukrainian Navy ships were closing out Exercise Lion Protector, demonstrating their ability to safely manoeuvre as a small task group in company with a major warship, played by Dauntless.

The apparent lack of new, organic sensors indicate that the interceptors must be receiving targeting data from the Type 45’s existing suite, i.e. the Sampson multi-function radar, the S1850M long-range radar on the aft mast and/or the electro optic systems.
Adapting to new threats The presence of this new system on a Type 45 destroyer shows how navies are adapting to the new challenges posed by affordable drones.
This suggests HMS Dauntless could be the first Type 45 ship to trial the capability ahead of her High North deployment.

Drone attack and swarming tactics—extensively practiced by the Royal Navy and French Navy in dedicated exercises like Sharpshooter and WildFire and based on their experience from Red Sea deployments—highlighted a critical limitation in European navies’ VLS magazine depth (48 cells for Type 45 and Horizon destroyers, 32 cells for French Air Defence FREMMs).
To address this issue, the Royal Navy started transitioning toward DragonFire lasers and C-UAS helicopter (Martlet / LMM aboard Wildcat) .

The new C-UAS system spotted on Dauntless shows that the Royal Navy continues to transform the Type 45 from a conventional air-defence vessel into a highly resilient platform capable of surviving drone saturation.

items.originalTitle: Hellenic Navy Tests SARONIC’s Corsair USV Ahead of Major Order
items.summary: The Hellenic Navy is currently testing a number of Corsair autonomous unmanned surface vessels (USVs) and has submitted a Letter of Request (LOR) to the United States for the procurement of at least 30 vessels to expand its unmanned maritime capabilities. On Tuesday, October 13, 2026, Greek Minister of National Defence Nikos Dendias attended the inauguration of the Joint Unmanned and Autonomous Maritime Systems Training Centre at the Palaskas Training Centre (KEPAL), part of the Hellenic Navy’s Naval Training Command.

evidenceRecords.text: The Hellenic Navy is currently testing a number of Corsair autonomous unmanned surface vessels (USVs) and has submitted a Letter of Request (LOR) to the United States for the procurement of at least 30 vessels to expand its unmanned maritime capabilities.

On Tuesday, October 13, 2026, Greek Minister of National Defence Nikos Dendias attended the inauguration of the Joint Unmanned and Autonomous Maritime Systems Training Centre at the Palaskas Training Centre (KEPAL), part of the Hellenic Navy’s Naval Training Command.

Photo taken during the inauguration of the Joint Unmanned and Autonomous Maritime Systems Training Centre at the Palaskas Training Centre, showing a Corsair USV (left) and the Hellenic Navy-developed Pyrpolitis USV (right).
However, the most notable highlight was a Corsair autonomous unmanned surface vehicle (USV) developed by US company Saronic .
According to a video released by the Ministry of National Defence (screenshots below), at least two Corsair USVs are currently in Greece undergoing trials with the Hellenic Navy.
The trials involved several Fleet units, with the fleet support ships HS Perseas (A377) and possibly HS Aias (A473) serving as motherships for transporting the unmanned vessels.
The trials also demonstrated the vessel’s ability to cooperate tactically with several warships.

Operating from HS Perseas Corsair USV and HS Perseas Corsair USV and HS Aias On the deck of HS Perseas The Ministry of National Defence stated that the Corsair USVs had undergone extensive trials and had been successfully evaluated by the Hellenic Navy.

A Letter of Request (LOR) has also been submitted to the United States for the procurement of an unspecified number of vessels through the government-to-government Foreign Military Sales (FMS) programme.
Separately, George Sideris of Hellas Journal reports that the Hellenic Navy plans to acquire at least 30 such vessels.
The reported procurement would form part of Greece’s ambition to significantly expand its USV capabilities in the near future.
Corsair USV Specifications The Corsair USV is capable of operating at ranges over 1,000 nautical miles and can support 1,000-pound payloads.

items.title: Launch Preview: Falcon 9, ZhuQue-2E to launch during quiet week
items.originalTitle: Launch Preview: Falcon 9, ZhuQue-2E to launch during quiet week
items.summary: This week features a relatively quiet launch manifest, with SpaceX’s workhorse Falcon 9 comprising much of the launch schedule. Three Falcon 9 missions will launch a cargo resupply mission to the International Space Station, a batch of satellites for SpaceX’s Starlink constellation, and a classified set of satellites for the United States Space Force. Furthermore, a Chinese ZhuQue-2E will launch an unknown payload to orbit. Falcon 9 | Starlink Group 15-25 The first scheduled launch of the week was a Falcon 9 from Vandenberg Space Force Base (VSFB) in California.

evidenceRecords.text: This week features a relatively quiet launch manifest, with SpaceX’s workhorse Falcon 9 comprising much of the launch schedule.

Three Falcon 9 missions will launch a cargo resupply mission to the International Space Station, a batch of satellites for SpaceX’s Starlink constellation, and a classified set of satellites for the United States Space Force.
Furthermore, a Chinese ZhuQue-2E will launch an unknown payload to orbit.
Falcon 9 | Starlink Group 15-25 The first scheduled launch of the week was a Falcon 9 from Vandenberg Space Force Base (VSFB) in California.
After liftoff from SLC-4E, Falcon 9 took a southeast trajectory and landed atop SpaceX’s autonomous droneship, Of Course I Still Love You , in the Pacific.
Falcon 9 is a 3.9 m-diameter, 70 m-tall two-stage rocket.
Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy were the first orbital rockets to achieve regular re-use, with one Falcon booster having flown as many as 37 flights.

Falcon 9 | CRS-35 A Falcon 9 launch from Cape Canaveral is now much less common following the transfer of Starlink launch duties to Starship; however, International Space Station (ISS) mission orbital mechanics fit well with east coast launch sites.
One such Falcon 9 mission was CRS-35, which launched on Tuesday, Oct. 13, at 6:33 AM EDT (10:33 UTC).
ZhuQue-2E | Unknown Payload A Chinese ZhuQue-2E rocket, developed by Landspace, is scheduled to launch on Wednesday, Oct. 14, at 11:40 UTC.
ZhuQue-2E will liftoff from Site 96A at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in China, with the launch window extending to 12:19 UTC.
Following launch, ZhuQue-2E will fly due south out of Jiuquan to deploy an unknown payload to an unknown orbit.

items.title: LaNeve to industry: ‘We are not walking away from modernization’
items.originalTitle: LaNeve to industry: ‘We are not walking away from modernization’
items.summary: The U.S. Army’s top officer sought to reassure industry leaders that the service remains committed to modernization and autonomous systems, announcing a new name for the command charged with shaping the future force during remarks at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington, D.C. Christopher LaNeve said that the Futures and Concepts Command has been redesignated as U.S. Army Futures and Autonomous Systems Command, or FASCOM.

evidenceRecords.text: The U.S. Army’s top officer sought to reassure industry leaders that the service remains committed to modernization and autonomous systems, announcing a new name for the command charged with shaping the future force during remarks at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington, D.C.
Christopher LaNeve said that the Futures and Concepts Command has been redesignated as U.S. Army Futures and Autonomous Systems Command, or FASCOM.

The change comes as the Army aligns its weapons purchases, force structure and training around new “How the Army Fights” guidance, which was published last week and explains how the service intends to wield land power in future wars.
“We are not walking away from modernization,” LaNeve said, addressing the industry partners directly at one point in his speech.

“We are sprinting towards, it,” he said, adding “and we are doing so responsibly with a recognition that resources are not endless.” LaNeve has charged FASCOM with developing corps-level autonomous capabilities through experimentation and testing.

According to a Tuesday release, the three-star command will have “capability-based formations centered on autonomous long-range fires, protection, tanks, logistics and obstacle breaching,” and will include some of the Army’s first 390A Robotic Technicians , which were activated this month.

“This goes beyond drones,” LaNeve said in the release, “FASCOM will pioneer operational concepts that harness autonomous capabilities across all warfighting functions.” The Army has come under fire recently after shuttering its experimental drone battalion in Europe less than a year after launching the novel unit to test how such a formation could operate.

items.originalTitle: Teledyne FLIR Defense launches mid-range C-UAS radar at AUSA 2026
items.summary: Teledyne FLIR Defense has announced the launch of Ranger® R10-3DX, a compact mid-range counter-unmanned aircraft system radar designed to provide advanced drone detection and tracking capabilities for military, security, and critical infrastructure operations. “The Ranger R10-3DX is engineered to support counter-drone, force protection, airport security, border security, coastal surveillance and other critical asset defence missions,” said the company in a press release.

evidenceRecords.text: Teledyne FLIR Defense has announced the launch of Ranger® R10-3DX, a compact mid-range counter-unmanned aircraft system radar designed to provide advanced drone detection and tracking capabilities for military, security, and critical infrastructure operations.

“The Ranger R10-3DX is engineered to support counter-drone, force protection, airport security, border security, coastal surveillance and other critical asset defence missions,” said the company in a press release.
“Using advanced digital beam-forming technology, the R10-3DX provides continuous wide-area coverage and rapid threat detection while maintaining a compact, low size, weight and power footprint.
Ranger R10-3DX can detect micro-UAS targets at ranges exceeding 3 kilometers, pedestrians beyond 6 kilometers, and light vehicles at more than 12 kilometers.

A single radar panel delivers 90-degree azimuth coverage and up to 60 degrees of elevation coverage, while a four-panel configuration provides full 360-degree surveillance.” “Small unmanned aircraft continue to present growing security challenges across military installations, airports, and other key infrastructure sites worldwide,” said Rob Tarantino, Senior Vice President of Surveillance at Teledyne FLIR Defense.

“The Ranger R10-3DX gives operators an affordable, compact, and highly capable radar solution that delivers the early warning and tracking performance needed to counter evolving drone threats.” The Ranger R10-3DX incorporates AI-based target classification algorithms that help users distinguish between drones, aircraft, birds, pedestrians and vehicles, enabling faster and more informed decision-making, says the company.

items.originalTitle: Houthi missile hits Aramco building after Saudi-led coalition strike on Yemen fuel depot

evidenceRecords.text: NASA astronaut Christina Koch stands inside Kennedy Space Center’s Vehicle Assembly Building on July 14, 2021, in front of the agency’s Space Launch System (SLS) rocket that ultimately powered the Orion spacecraft on the Artemis I mission.
Koch later served as a crew member on the Artemis II mission in 2026, and on Oct. 13, 2026, NASA announced she will serve next as the agency’s acting deputy chief engineer.

NASA/Glenn Benson NASA engineer and astronaut Christina Koch will serve as the agency’s acting deputy chief engineer beginning on Sunday, Nov. 1, following the retirement of Katherine Van Hooser, who will conclude more than 35 years of distinguished service to the agency on Wednesday, Oct. 21.
In her new role, Koch will help lead NASA’s engineering community, supporting technical oversight, mission readiness, and engineering excellence across the agency’s programs and projects.
With this appointment, Koch will transition to management astronaut status and will no longer be eligible for future spaceflight assignments.
“Christina has seen NASA engineering from both sides of the equation: developing complex systems on the ground and trusting them with her life in space,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman.

“After spending nearly a year living and working aboard the International Space Station and helping lead America back around the Moon on Artemis II this year, she brings an extraordinary combination of technical expertise, operational experience, and judgment to this role.

I am excited to see the impact she will have across NASA as we return Americans to the lunar surface, build the Moon Base, get underway on nuclear power in space, and develop the capabilities that will ultimately take us on to Mars.” “Katherine has been an extraordinary leader throughout her career, bringing technical expertise, sound judgment, and an unwavering commitment to mission success to some of NASA’s most complex engineering challenges,” said Amit Kshatriya, NASA associate administrator and chief engineer.
“Her leadership has strengthened our engineering community and helped guide the agency through critical milestones and transitions.
As Marshall’s chief engineer and, since 2023, NASA’s deputy chief engineer, Van Hooser provided critical technical leadership and oversight across the agency’s programs.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief Manipal Academy of Higher Education launched Manipal House of Quantum, Quantum-Hub@MAHE, at MIT Bengaluru to support quantum engineering, hardware experimentation and indigenous technology development in India.
PRESS RELEASE — Manipal Institute of Technology, Bengaluru (MIT Bengaluru) on Tuesday launched Manipal House of Quantum, Quantum-Hub@MAHE.
Venkatesh, VSM (Retd.), 7th Vice Chancellor, MAHE and Advisor to MEMG; Prof. (Dr.) Madhu Veeraraghavan, Pro Vice Chancellor, MAHE Bengaluru; Dr. Karunakar A.

Kotegar, Pro Vice Chancellor, Technology & Science, MAHE; Dr. Raghavendra Prabhu, Additional Registrar, MAHE Bengaluru; Prof. Iven Jose, Director, MIT Bengaluru; and Mr. Vishal Chatrath, Co-Founder & CEO, QuantrolOX .

Located at the MAHE Bengaluru campus, the quantum facility at MIT Bengaluru provides students, researchers and industry collaborators with hands-on access to advanced quantum computing infrastructure, including quantum hardware, cryogenic systems and quantum control technologies.

Through an integrated academic framework, the facility will support experimentation, application development, deep-tech start-up incubation, component innovation, testing and translational research, positioning MIT Bengaluru as an emerging centre for quantum engineering and indigenous hardware development.
The facility commences operations with a 25-qubit open-architecture dilution refrigeration system designed for advanced training and experimentation.
Rao, Vice Chancellor, MAHE, said, “The MAHE House of Quantum at MIT Bengaluru reflects MAHE’s commitment to building advanced scientific capabilities and nurturing talent in emerging technologies.

By creating access to modern quantum infrastructure, we aim to contribute meaningfully to India’s growing quantum ecosystem.” Prof. (Dr.) Madhu Veeraraghavan, Pro Vice Chancellor, MAHE Bengaluru, said, “The Hub brings together education, research and innovation on a common platform.

It will create opportunities for interdisciplinary collaboration and help translate academic research into real-world technological impact.” Prof. Iven Jose, Director, MIT Bengaluru, said, “The quantum facility at MIT Bengaluru will provide students and researchers with valuable exposure to real quantum systems and engineering environments.

It marks an important step towards developing the next generation of quantum scientists, engineers and innovators.” Ahead of the launch, faculty members and students from the Bengaluru and Manipal campuses completed specialised training at the MIT Bengaluru campus and the QuantrolOx laboratory at QuTech, TU Delft, in the Netherlands.

The programme developed practical capabilities in dilution refrigerator assembly, cryogenic systems, quantum control technologies, QPU measurements and superconducting quantum hardware, preparing the team to support the operations of the quantum facility at MIT Bengaluru.

items.title: Anduril reveals family of surface-to-air interceptor missiles
items.originalTitle: Anduril reveals family of surface-to-air interceptor missiles
items.summary: Anduril released a new family of surface-to-air interceptor missiles in an effort to create a more diverse range of defensive measures while building at scale. Steelfin, a family of highly configurable, mass-producible, surface-to-air interceptor missiles, has been developed to deliver cost, volume and capability across a variety of threats, according to a release .

evidenceRecords.text: Anduril released a new family of surface-to-air interceptor missiles in an effort to create a more diverse range of defensive measures while building at scale.

Steelfin, a family of highly configurable, mass-producible, surface-to-air interceptor missiles, has been developed to deliver cost, volume and capability across a variety of threats, according to a release .

Steefin uses a two-stage architecture compatible with different fielded designs, allowing the defense company to configure interceptor performance while reusing the same parts, production processes, and design across its family of interceptors.
The missile has a two-stage design with a booster and terminal interceptor, the release states.
The first-stage booster can accommodate various solid rocket motor boosters to meet a set range, performance, booster types, launch configurations or packing density requirements.
The second stage terminal interceptor shares the same baseline airframe, avionics, software, flight control system and interfaces across all Steelfin variants.
“Steelfin delivers a diversity of effects to meet a diversity of threats,” the release says.

“Unlike legacy missiles that carry fixed, inflexible designs that are resistant to change, Steelfin offers a common interceptor architecture that produces a family of interceptor missiles, each of which can be configured for a specific mission.” The interceptor family was built to address threats across the air-and-missile defense spectrum, such as point defense, integrated air and missile defense and ballistic missile defense, while aiming to come at a fraction of the cost of other interceptors in mission classes.

To address issues with manufacturing volume and high demand, Anduril expects to “surge” production for any Steelfin variant by moving the interceptor through the same production line, with the same tooling, techniques and facilities, since they share a common architecture and components.
Anduril anticipates producing several thousand Steelfin variants per year in the short term, the announcement says.
Steelfin is meant to be able to integrate with any fielded fire control software systems, like AEGIS and IBCS, to ensure it fits into established battle management processes and procedures.

HD Hyundai Heavy Industries press release Marking another milestone in a decade-long defense partnership, HD Hyundai Heavy Industries (HD HHI) launched the BRP Rajah Humabon , the third of six 2,400-ton Offshore Patrol Vessels (OPVs) built for the Philippine Navy, at its primary shipyard in Ulsan on Monday.

HD Hyundai Heavy Industries press release Marking another milestone in a decade-long defense partnership, HD Hyundai Heavy Industries (HD HHI) launched the BRP Rajah Humabon , the third of six 2,400-ton Offshore Patrol Vessels (OPVs) built for the Philippine Navy, at its primary shipyard in Ulsan on Monday.
The ceremonial launching—HD HHI’s first export naval vessel launch of the year—was attended by prominent diplomatic and military leaders from both nations, including Vice Admiral Jose Ma.
Ambrosio Ezpeleta, Flag Officer in Command of the Philippine Navy; Bernadette Therese Fernandez, Philippine Ambassador to South Korea; Lieutenant General Rommel P.
Roldan, Vice Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces of the Philippines; and Won-ho Joo, President & Head of Naval & Medium Size Ships Business Unit at HD HHI.
Named after the 16th-century ruler of Cebu who played a pivotal role in early Philippine history, the Rajah Humabon is scheduled for official delivery in February 2027.
BRP Rajah Humabon launching ceremony.

Advanced Maritime Capabilities Designed to enhance maritime domain awareness and coastal defense capabilities across the Philippine archipelago, the state-of-the-art 2,400-ton vessel measures 94 meters in length and 14 meters in width.

Capable of maintaining a cruising speed of 15 knots (approximately 28 km/h) with an impressive operational range of 5,500 nautical miles (10,186 km), the patrol ship is built for extended endurance at sea.
The vessel is equipped with advanced defense systems, including a 76mm main naval gun, a 30mm secondary gun, decoy launching systems, surveillance radar, and electro-optical tracking equipment.
A Decade of Naval Partnership The launch of the Rajah Humabon marks a decade of continuous naval cooperation between HD HHI and the Philippine Armed Forces.
The relationship began in 2016 with a milestone contract for the Philippine Navy’s first modern frigates.

items.originalTitle: Saudi Arabia strikes oil depots in Yemen and says missiles launched toward location of Saudi Aramco HQ
items.summary: Saudi Arabia has launched a series of strikes on a strategic oil depot on the outskirts of Yemen’s capital, Sana’a, while later on Tuesday it said it had intercepted missiles launched toward Dharan, location of the headquarters of the huge national energy company Saudi Aramco. The attacks on both sides were a fresh escalation of the conflict between Riyadh and the Iran-backed Houthi forces.

evidenceRecords.text: Civilians warned to leave target area near Sana’a before attacks as conflict between Riyadh and Houthi forces escalates Saudi Arabia has launched a series of strikes on a strategic oil depot on the outskirts of Yemen’s capital, Sana’a, while later on Tuesday it said it had intercepted missiles launched toward Dharan, location of the headquarters of the huge national energy company Saudi Aramco.
The attacks on both sides were a fresh escalation of the conflict between Riyadh and the Iran-backed Houthi forces.

Before its offensive on Tuesday, a Saudi spokesperson warned civilians to leave the target area, in an apparent attempt to strike fear into the local population before the biggest attack so far on Houthi energy infrastructure.

Saudi Arabia has launched a series of strikes on a strategic oil depot on the outskirts of Yemen’s capital, Sana’a, while later on Tuesday it said it had intercepted missiles launched toward Dharan, location of the headquarters of the huge national energy company Saudi Aramco.

The Central Sabaha Station oil depot on the western side of the city contains large tanks that often hold substantial quantities of fuel derivatives, although the Yemeni Oil Company said its storage facilities were empty at the time of the attack.

Houthi oil depots at the Ras Isa port in Hodeidah, the subject of Israeli attacks in 2024, were also struck in 10 waves of attacks apparently aimed at immobilising the Houthi army as it continues its push south, including towards the city of Taiz.
Earlier the Saudis also struck what they believe to be a Houthi leadership hide-out in the Bani Mu’in area in the Razih border district, west of Saada governorate, northern Yemen.
The strike on the oil depot appeared to be the Saudi response to a Houthi attack on King Khalid international airport in Riyadh on Saturday that killed 13 people and left 300 injured.
The airport is closed until Saturday at the earliest, a blow to an economy that is trying to show its security makes the country a safe place to invest.
The incident underlined how Saudi Arabia has complete air dominance over Yemen while the Houthis have to reply using drones and missiles which can be intercepted.
Baraa Shiban, a Yemen specialist at the defence thinktank Royal United Services Institute (Rusi), warned “Saudi Arabia is struggling to respond to the Houthi’s improved arms technology.
Until relatively recently Houthi missiles and drones fell in desert areas or if they got through were intercepted.
They have learned how to deploy drones that fly lower and are smaller, and are less easy to detect.

items.originalTitle: Sikorsky Aiming For Black Hawk ‘Nose Jobs’ To Be Available Within The Next Year
items.summary: Sikorsky is aiming to start offering a new modular and readily swappable nose for the venerable H-60 family of helicopters within the next year or so. The noses will be made available on new-production H-60s, as well as be retrofittable to helicopters in service now. The ‘nose jobs’ will help operators relatively quickly reconfigure their H-60s for very different missions, from cargo-carrying to serving as gunships , as required.

The ‘nose jobs’ will help operators relatively quickly reconfigure their H-60s for very different missions, from cargo-carrying to serving as gunships , as required.

Our Howard Altman had a chance to speak with representatives from Sikorsky, now a subsidiary of Lockheed Martin, about the plans for the new nose for the H-60-series at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention today.
Within the next, I would say, year or so, the nose will be available to be retrofitted or to be coming off the line,” Jason Wrigley, Sikorsky’s director of business development for Black Hawk, said.

“The new modular nose will change the look of the Black Hawk up front to provide even more space for equipment that will work directly with the new digital architecture.” In terms of swapping out modular noses on individual helicopters, Wrigley said that it is still too early in the design process to know exactly how that would be done and how long it might take to do so in practice.

items.title: SEALSQ Presents Research on Side-Channel Attacks Against ML-KEM
items.originalTitle: SEALSQ Presents Research on Side-Channel Attacks Against ML-KEM
items.summary: Insider Brief SEALSQ presented peer-reviewed research at LightSec 2026 on a side-channel attack targeting the encoding step of ML-KEM key generation, along with countermeasures to reduce implementation vulnerabilities. The research combines profiling-based techniques with lattice reduction to recover sensitive information from side-channel leakage under realistic conditions.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief SEALSQ presented peer-reviewed research at LightSec 2026 on a side-channel attack targeting the encoding step of ML-KEM key generation, along with countermeasures to reduce implementation vulnerabilities.
The research combines profiling-based techniques with lattice reduction to recover sensitive information from side-channel leakage under realistic conditions.

The work examines implementation risks in NIST-standardized post-quantum cryptography and complements SEALSQ ’s hardware security development, including its QS7001 secure element, which is undergoing Common Criteria EAL5+ certification.

PRESS RELEASE — SEALSQ Corp (NASDAQ: LAES) (“SEALSQ” or “Company”), a company that focuses on developing and selling Semiconductors, PKI, and Post-Quantum technology hardware and software products, today announced that its research team presented a peer-reviewed technical article on a novel side-channel attack targeting the encoding step of ML-KEM (Module-Lattice-Based Key Encapsulation Mechanism, formerly CRYSTALS-Kyber) key generation at LightSec 2026.

LightSec 2026, the 7 th International Workshop on Lightweight Cryptography for Security & Privacy, took place on October 11, 2026, in Antalya, Turkey, as an official affiliated event of CHES 2026 (Conference on Cryptographic Hardware and Embedded Systems), the premier venue for research on the design and analysis of cryptographic hardware and embedded systems.
The paper, titled “Cross-information lattice attack on ML-KEM,” demonstrates how the encoding step during ML-KEM key generation is vulnerable to side-channel attacks under realistic conditions.
The work introduces a novel attack method that combines profiling-based techniques with lattice reduction.
The researchers also present practical countermeasures designed to improve the robustness of ML-KEM implementations against such attacks.
This contribution highlights SEALSQ ’s position at the vanguard of cryptographic hardware technology.

By rigorously analyzing and hardening implementations of NIST-standardized algorithms such as ML-KEM (FIPS 203), the company helps advance the state of the art in secure architectures that must withstand both mathematical cryptanalysis and physical implementation attacks.

items.title: Lockheed eyes fresh PAC-3 interceptor production options for Ukraine, Europe
items.originalTitle: Lockheed eyes fresh PAC-3 interceptor production options for Ukraine, Europe
items.summary: Lockheed Martin is weighing new industry partnerships to produce urgently needed PAC-3 Patriot interceptors in Europe, an avenue that could also help fill Ukraine’s shortfalls, a company executive said. Discussions about producing more Patriot interceptors outside the United States have picked up steam since Ukrainian leaders said over the summer they were promised by the Trump administration a license to make them in Ukraine to defend against Russian missile and drone barrages.

evidenceRecords.text: Lockheed Martin is weighing new industry partnerships to produce urgently needed PAC-3 Patriot interceptors in Europe, an avenue that could also help fill Ukraine’s shortfalls, a company executive said.

Discussions about producing more Patriot interceptors outside the United States have picked up steam since Ukrainian leaders said over the summer they were promised by the Trump administration a license to make them in Ukraine to defend against Russian missile and drone barrages.
U.S. government officials are still expected to make a decision, which could entail the production of PAC-2 interceptors, made by Raytheon, or Lockheed’s PAC-3.

“From a PAC-3 perspective, we’re absolutely willing to talk to Ukraine,” Jason Reynolds, vice president and general manager of the company’s integrated air and missile defense division, told Defense News in an interview at the Association of the United States Army annual convention in Washington, DC.

Patriot interceptor deliveries to Poland will be delayed, top general says “It’s really a matter of what’s their industrial capability, what’s the parts availability, those types of things,” he continued.

“It might be something like an ACE, as opposed to an MSE, that we would start with for Ukraine.” Lockheed announced development of an ACE variant during the summer, billing it as a cheaper option against relatively simple threats — at half the cost of an MSE missile designed to go against sophisticated missiles.

The new interceptor will make do with a single-pulse motor, compared with a dual-pulse of the MSE interceptor, and utilize a blast fragmentation warhead, versus the direct hit-to-kill mechanics of the MSE missile.
Reynolds cautioned that setting up interceptor missile production of whatever variant in Ukraine comes with the risk of Russian attacks on the plant.

“If we can get that started, get the supply chain started and then migrate to Ukraine as an option, that would make a lot of sense to me.” Germany is among the countries where leaders have offered to host PAC-3 production .

For an eventual PAC-3 production, Lockheed is considering partnering with Diehl Defence, with which there is a cooperation agreement on interceptor parts in place dating from October 2025, Reynolds said.

PRESS RELEASE — Bristol-based Siloton has been awarded a major contract to accelerate the development of its groundbreaking handheld eye imaging system, which makes the detection and monitoring of retinal diseases more accessible to patients.
The med-tech start-up has secured £8.4 million from Innovate UK, part of UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), through its Contracts for Innovation: Quantum Missions Primer initiative.

Delivered over two years, the contract will help Siloton accelerate the design of the in-clinic and at-home versions of its GiraffeOCT optical coherence tomography (OCT) device, as well as complete trials on both systems.
The start-up expects the funding could cut the development process by up to two years.

Siloton will work with Sunderland Specialist Eye Hospital on clinical trials over the course of the contract for its in-clinic device, giving patients across the North East and North Cumbria access to the technology during its development.

items.originalTitle: Ukraine and NATO develop AI model to predict enemy drone attacks
items.summary: Ukraine and NATO have developed an artificial intelligence model designed to predict enemy drone attacks near the line of contact, using historical data, weather conditions and the current battlefield situation, according to the Ukrainian ministry of defence. Code-named Model No. 13, the tool was jointly developed by NATO’s Allied Command Transformation (ACT) and the Armed Forces of Ukraine, with support from the NATO-Ukraine Joint Analysis, Training and Education Centre (JATEC).

Rickey Jackson, command sergeant major of the U.S. Army Space and Missile Defense Command, said in the release.

“We had nearly 3,000 soldiers apply, and selected over 600 of the most capable, professional soldiers in the Army,” Command Sgt.
Rickey Jackson, command sergeant major of the U.S. Army Space and Missile Defense Command, said in the release.

“Ultimately, we are looking for soldiers who master their current jobs and consistently stand apart from their peers.” The Army announced in January that it was opening applications for the specialty to soldiers in grades E-4 through E-9 across the active-duty Army, National Guard and Army Reserve.
Previously, the service temporarily pulled soldiers from other specialties to help with space operations.
However, the soldiers’ experience was often lost when they returned to their original branches.
“For too long, enlisted soldiers with specialized space training and experience rotated through critical space assignments, eventually returning to their basic branches,” Lt.

“The rotational system served the U.S. Army well in the past but will not meet the demands of the future, which requires a professional and sustainable approach to training, career progression and leader development for Army Space soldiers.

The Army’s Space Operations Branch was officially established in June, bringing together the newly-created enlisted occupational specialty and functional area 40As, the Army’s Space Operations Officers.

“Our space operations soldiers bring unmatched value to the Army and joint force because of the education and training they receive to execute space integration and interdiction missions — specifically counter-SATCOM, stratospheric warfare, navigation warfare and counter-sensing,” Col.
Space systems, the Army said, help soldiers with navigation, weather, communication and early warnings.

However, what we’ve seen is, with the environment as it is, everything that we produce as a capable counter-UAS system tends to get deployed somewhere,” said Kirk Williams, chief engineer at the U.S. Army Directed Energy Project Office.
In September, the Army awarded AeroVironment a $464.8 million contract for LOCUST X3, its modular, palletized high-energy laser system.
Earlier generations of the LOCUST system are actively fielded in operational environments, including at the U.S. southern border, according to AeroVironment.
The first LOCUST X3 is slated for delivery by Q4 of FY 2027 and will be mounted on the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle.
That would be a great win for the Army.” It is unclear where the first high-energy counter-drone weapons under H-ELS will be deployed.

The counter-drone E-HEL contract is for more than 26 laser weapons units total, according to AeroVironment vice president of Directed Energy, John Garrity, who indicated the initial system is on target for 2027 delivery.
“We would love to be able to keep the first unit off the line for our testing and training.
The goal is to push it through testing, validation, verification and “give it to soldiers as soon as possible,” said Brig.
Gen. Guy Yelverton, capability program executive for Defensive Fires. “My far-down point would be spring [2028], and if I could get in the December-January timeframe, that would be awesome.
That would be a great win for the Army.”
It is unclear where the first high-energy counter-drone weapons under H-ELS will be deployed.
Yelverton suggested the 7th Infantry Division could be a potential partner.

Deputy commanding officer of Support for the 7th Infantry Division, Col. Charles Kean, described directed-energy weapons as a component of defense against high-echelon air threats, including individual UAS or formations, but said they were not a “single bullet” solution.

items.title: QFX Wins £6.8 Million Innovate UK Contract for Quantum Timing Hardware
items.originalTitle: QFX Wins £6.8 Million Innovate UK Contract for Quantum Timing Hardware
items.summary: Insider Brief QFX, an Oxford University spinout, has secured a £6.8 million Innovate UK contract to develop atomic and vacuum hardware for data centre timing and space applications. The SrROCK Phase II programme will build a compact, low-power strontium optical-clock package, demonstrate its timing performance and conduct testing relevant to future satellite missions. The programme aims to establish UK manufacturing capacity and intellectual property for advanced atomic and vacuum systems while supporting QFX’s development of distributed quantum computing and networking hardware.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief QFX, an Oxford University spinout, has secured a £6.8 million Innovate UK contract to develop atomic and vacuum hardware for data centre timing and space applications.
The SrROCK Phase II programme will build a compact, low-power strontium optical-clock package, demonstrate its timing performance and conduct testing relevant to future satellite missions.

The programme aims to establish UK manufacturing capacity and intellectual property for advanced atomic and vacuum systems while supporting QFX’s development of distributed quantum computing and networking hardware.

PRESS RELEASE — QFX (Quantum Fabrix Ltd), an Oxford University spinout developing hardware infrastructure for distributed quantum computing and quantum networking, has been awarded a £6.8 million contract by Innovate UK to deliver Phase II of its SrROCK development programme.
Building on a successful first phase, SrROCK will advance QFX’s atomic source and vacuum technologies into robust, integrated hardware for data centre and space applications.
QFX’s technology platform combines atomic sources, ultra-high-vacuum systems and quantum interfaces in a modular architecture for demanding data centre and space applications.
This approach gives QFX access to near-term opportunities in timing and navigation while building towards fault-tolerant distributed quantum computing.
“SrROCK gives QFX the opportunity to prove that its core atomic and vacuum technologies can be manufactured and qualified for demanding real-world applications.

That capability is essential to scaling our quantum-computing platform and creates a clear route into the strategically important timing market, supporting sovereign UK supply of advanced timing technology.” Dr Timothy Ballance , CEO, QFX In Phase II, QFX will engineer and integrate a compact, low-power strontium optical-clock physics package for timing infrastructure in data centres and future satellite missions.
The programme will demonstrate timing performance and complete space-relevant testing, generating the evidence needed for customer adoption and future space qualification.

Engagement with data centre operators, spacecraft manufacturers, mission operators and end users will define deployment requirements, commercial pathways and plans for a subsequent space demonstration.

items.title: DroneShield announces Q4 software update for counter-drone systems
items.originalTitle: DroneShield announces Q4 software update for counter-drone systems
items.summary: DroneShield has announced a fourth-quarter software release designed to improve drone detection, identification, tracking and defeat capabilities across its counter-unmanned aircraft systems. The update introduces a feature that flags unfamiliar radio-frequency signals exhibiting drone-like characteristics, allowing operators to investigate potential new threats that are not yet included in DroneShield’s threat library. It also improves thermal camera classification accuracy by 44%, while fixed-wing drone identification precision increases by 18% and recall by 8%, according to the company.

evidenceRecords.text: DroneShield has announced a fourth-quarter software release designed to improve drone detection, identification, tracking and defeat capabilities across its counter-unmanned aircraft systems.
It also improves thermal camera classification accuracy by 44%, while fixed-wing drone identification precision increases by 18% and recall by 8%, according to the company.
The release also enables radio-frequency sensors and compatible optical cameras to work together for passive detection and visual confirmation.
With compatible Bosch Starlight cameras, operators can direct cameras towards the source of an RF detection before locking on to and tracking a drone.

For threat mitigation, connected DroneSentry-X Mk2 units can share detections to coordinate disruption, while jamming can be focused on frequencies used by the specific drone to reduce interference with nearby systems.

DroneShield said the software is available through its Mission Ready Services subscription, enabling compatible equipment already in the field to receive capability improvements without new hardware investment.
The DroneSentry-C2 software release is scheduled to become available on 3 November 2026.

The company said its subscription supports more than 4,200 software-enabled devices.

The system combines Active Electronically Scanned Array (AESA) radar technology with an elevated aerostat platform to extend detection range beyond terrain and other ground-level obstructions. It is designed to detect and track multiple aerial, maritime and ground targets.

evidenceRecords.text: Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) has unveiled POINT@AIR, a mobile aerostat-based radar designed to provide persistent surveillance and long-range detection, at the Association of the United States Army (AUSA) Annual Meeting and Exposition in Washington, DC.
The system combines Active Electronically Scanned Array (AESA) radar technology with an elevated aerostat platform to extend detection range beyond terrain and other ground-level obstructions.
Based on IAI’s ELM-2083 radar family, POINT@AIR combines electronic scanning in azimuth and elevation with mechanical rotation to provide 360-degree coverage.
The mobile system is designed for persistent operation and rapid relocation without relying on permanent infrastructure.

IAI said the radar can support multiple missions simultaneously, prioritise targets according to operational requirements and interface with command-and-control systems to contribute to a shared operational picture.

items.originalTitle: Qilimanjaro Quantum Tech Announces Nearly €20 Million First Close of Series A Led by Indra Group
items.summary: Insider Brief Qilimanjaro Quantum Tech completed a €19.6 million –about $22 million USD — first close of its Series A round, with €10 million from Indra Group through IndraMind and €9.6 million from Spain’s SETT . The funding will support scaling and industrializing its quantum computers, developing new chips and expanding manufacturing and deployment capacity. The Barcelona-based company has deployed eight quantum systems, including three integrated with the Barcelona Supercomputing Center, and expects to complete the funding round in the fourth quarter.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief Qilimanjaro Quantum Tech completed a €19.6 million –about $22 million USD — first close of its Series A round, with €10 million from Indra Group through IndraMind and €9.6 million from Spain’s SETT .
The funding will support scaling and industrializing its quantum computers, developing new chips and expanding manufacturing and deployment capacity.
The Barcelona-based company has deployed eight quantum systems, including three integrated with the Barcelona Supercomputing Center, and expects to complete the funding round in the fourth quarter.

PRESS RELEASE — Qilimanjaro Quantum Tech has completed a €19.6 million — about $22 million USD — first close of its Series A funding round, led by Indra Group through IndraMind with a €10 million investment.

The Spanish Society for Technological Transformation (SETT) , under the Ministry for Digital Transformation and Public Administration, is also renewing its commitment to the company with a new €9.6 million investment.

Indra Group is investing in Qilimanjaro through an instrument that will convert upon the closing of the round, while SETT is reinforcing its support for the company after having participated in its previous funding round.

The new capital will enable Qilimanjaro to scale and industrialize its quantum computers, advance the development of new generations of chips, and increase its manufacturing and deployment capacity, strengthening a technological capability developed in Spain and contributing to greater European technological autonomy in quantum computing.
“SETT’s renewed commitment and Indra ’s investment bring sovereign and industrial capital together to protect, while also accelerating, national technological autonomy.

Together, we are joining forces to bring quantum computing closer to strategic industrial sectors and to ensure that the quantum technology being built in Spain continues to grow in Spain,” said Marta P.
Estarellas, CEO of Qilimanjaro Quantum Tech.

With this transaction, Indra Group strengthens its position in this strategic field, while IndraMind expands the capabilities it can use to develop sovereign, differentiated solutions for defense, security and industry,” said Ignacio Martínez, General Manager of IndraMind.
Founded in Barcelona in 2019, Qilimanjaro is Spain’s only full-stack quantum computing company.

evidenceRecords.text: WARSAW, Poland — Norway’s Kongsberg has decided to build a new production facility for counter-drone systems in northern Poland, with plans to invest more than 200 million zloty ($51 million) in the plant.
The investment is connected to the company’s cooperation with Polish state-run defense group PGZ to deliver the San anti-drone system to the Polish military.
“We have been present in Poland for many years.

We think it’s important that we establish local sites in Poland,” Eirik Lie, the president and CEO of Kongsberg, told Defense News at the Warsaw Security Forum here on Oct. 12. “We are on good track for deliveries on the San program.
But also, we expect export contracts, so this enables us to be prepared for these exports from Poland.”

Under the San deal, valued at around PLN 15 billion ($3.8 billion), Kongsberg and PGZ are to supply 18 anti-drone batteries, 52 firing platoons, 18 command platoons, and 703 vehicles to the Polish military, according to data from Poland’s Ministry of National Defence.
The contract will be largely financed by loans that Poland has secured from the European Union’s Security Action For Europe (SAFE) scheme.
In a statement, the Norwegian group said it plans to sign a construction contract by the end of 2026 and begin work immediately afterward.
Serial production of counter-drone systems could begin in the first half of 2028.
The investment is expected to create more than 100 jobs in Poland once the plant reaches full capacity.

evidenceRecords.text: General Dynamics Land Systems is showcasing a 1/8 model of the Wolf XM30, the company’s candidate to replace the M2 Bradley, along with PERCH 2.0, M-SHORAD Increment 4 and the F600 Leonidas at the Association of the United States Army’s annual meeting this week.
The Wolf is one of two vehicles competing in the Army’s XM30 program , with American Rheinmetall delivering its first Lynx XM30 prototype to the Army in September.

Retired Army officer Scott Taylor, General Dynamics Land Systems’ director of U.S. growth, told Military Times that the Bradley has reached the limits of its ability to accommodate additional capabilities and weight.
The Wolf is designed with greater capacity in mind, while improving fightability, lethality and survivability, Taylor said.
General Dynamics Land Systems delivered its first Wolf prototype to the Army in August.
PERCH 2.0 allows M1A2 Abrams main battle tanks and Stryker vehicles to launch Switchblade 300 loitering munitions while keeping operators under armor.
One PERCH 2.0 prototype has been provided to the Army for experimentation, with three more on the way.
Soldiers with 2nd Battalion, 12th Cavalry Regiment, 1st Brigade Combat Team, known as “Thunder Horse,” are currently testing the prototype at Fort Hood, Texas, Taylor noted.

The system grew out of General Dynamics Land Systems’ development of PERCH 1.0, which the company developed in less than four months after senior Army leaders discussed observations from the war in Ukraine during a 2025 event, Taylor said.
The Army initially experimented with Switchblade 600 before asking the company to focus on the smaller Switchblade 300, according to Taylor.

General Dynamics Land Systems continued developing PERCH 2.0 with its own independent research and development funding before the Army contracted for three additional prototypes under the Abrams program office.
The Army will evaluate the design after the experimentation and could compete the capability or purchase it, depending on the results, Taylor explained.

items.originalTitle: The US military’s race to make fake blood
items.summary: Today, a chronic shortage of blood in both the military and civilian worlds is fueling a race to develop synthetic alternatives. items.originalTitle: Ukrainian soldier goes on trial over sabotage of Nord Stream gas pipelines
items.summary: A Ukrainian soldier has gone on trial in Hamburg accused of taking part in one of the most brazen acts of sabotage in postwar European history – the 2022 attack on the Nord Stream gas pipelines between Russia and Germany. Serhii Kuznetsov, a special forces officer from the Ukrainian military, is accused by prosecutors of being an accomplice to war crimes by attacking civilian infrastructure, causing an explosion, damaging property and disrupting public services.

evidenceRecords.text: Special forces officer Serhii Kuznetsov denies involvement in the 2022 blasts that left pipelines badly damaged A Ukrainian soldier has gone on trial in Hamburg accused of taking part in one of the most brazen acts of sabotage in postwar European history – the 2022 attack on the Nord Stream gas pipelines between Russia and Germany.

Serhii Kuznetsov, a special forces officer from the Ukrainian military, is accused by prosecutors of being an accomplice to war crimes by attacking civilian infrastructure, causing an explosion, damaging property and disrupting public services.

A Ukrainian soldier has gone on trial in Hamburg accused of taking part in one of the most brazen acts of sabotage in postwar European history – the 2022 attack on the Nord Stream gas pipelines between Russia and Germany.
The blasts caused the Nord Stream 1 pipelines – Russia’s main gas supply route to Germany before Moscow cut the supplies in August 2022 – to burst.
They also damaged Nord Stream 2, which was ready to carry gas but was never put into operation after Germany suspended its authorisation process just before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

However, in July German state prosecutors accused Ukrainian “state authorities” of ordering the attack, arguing: “The aim was to permanently halt gas supplies via the pipelines and prevent Russia from using the revenue from natural gas trade to finance its war effort.”
The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has denied his country was involved.

The far-right populist, pro-Kremlin Alternative für Deutschland party, which is soaring in the polls, has seized on the Nord Stream plot to boost its argument that German aid for Ukraine must cease and the pipeline be reinstated so that cheap supplies of gas can help counter the cost of living crisis.

The pro-Ukrainian protesters who turned out on Wednesday were just a few feet away from a group of supporters of the far-left BSW party, which echoes the AfD’s stance on Russia and would also like to see the pipelines reinstated.
They were holding placards demanding a parliamentary inquiry to investigate the political motives behind the Nord Stream attack.
Kuznetsov’s defence team is expected to argue that the trial should not be taking place at all, and that the defendant is being treated “like a pawn on a chessboard”.

They have indicated they would like proceedings to address the question of whether it is right to view the Nord Stream pipelines as civilian energy infrastructure, as they have been portrayed by the German state, or whether the operation had a military objective from the outset.

items.title: BAE Systems unveils new layered air-defense system
items.originalTitle: BAE Systems unveils new layered air-defense system
items.summary: BAE Systems unveiled new layered air-defense systems designed to counter missiles and drones on Monday at the annual meeting of the Association of the United States Army. The international defense company introduced the Multi-Domain Artillery Cannon System, or MDACS, and the High-Power Microwave, or HPM, as complementary systems for protecting critical installations and field units.

evidenceRecords.text: BAE Systems unveiled new layered air-defense systems designed to counter missiles and drones on Monday at the annual meeting of the Association of the United States Army.

The international defense company introduced the Multi-Domain Artillery Cannon System, or MDACS, and the High-Power Microwave, or HPM, as complementary systems for protecting critical installations and field units.

Travis Langer, BAE Systems’ communication manager, explained to Military Times that the systems together fill a capability gap created by evolving technological threats and the military’s traditional procurement process.

“Both products complement existing air defense systems, but each offer a more cost-effective solution for defense against high-volume, low-cost threats allowing the preservation of high-value missiles for the most critical targets, which extends the life and effectiveness of the entire missile stockpile,” Langer said.

The Multi-Domain Artillery Cannon System According to BAE Systems, MDACS forms the kinetic layer of the defensive shield, using precision-guided munitions called Hypervelocity Projectiles, or HVPs, for both offensive and defensive operations.

“It fills a gap that traditional artillery cannot, providing a scalable layer of protection that complements existing high-tier systems,” Langer said, adding that it allows the Defense Department “to maintain a sustainable defense without draining the budget on every single engagement.” He explained MDACS combines high-accuracy guidance with the extreme velocity of the HVP.
BAE Systems secured an Army agreement to develop a prototype of MDACS in January 2025, according to reports .
The High-Power Microwave BAE Systems describes its HPM system as a “scalable directed energy weapon” built with an emphasis on affordability.
Although the system remains in the prototype stage, BAE Systems said it has reached Technology Readiness Level 6, or TRL 6.
Layered air-defense Langer explained that the two systems are not specifically designed to be used together, but they could complement each other if the mission set requires it.

PRESS RELEASE — Classiq , a leading quantum computing software company, and FreeYa Mind Campus by S.C.

Extensive Network SRL today announced a strategic commercial agreement to build quantum application development, education, enterprise and national capabilities at the campus’s hardware-enabled Quantum AI center in Iași, Romania.
Under the agreement, FreeYa Mind Campus will offer access to Classiq ’s enterprise-grade quantum software platform , both on campus and across the Romanian ecosystem.

Working with the campus team, Classiq will connect quantum innovation to real-world industry applications.
The campus will offer university curriculum materials, practitioner training, enterprise onboarding, advanced application development and Classiq certification resources.
To support customer engagement, project execution and application delivery, Classiq will establish its Romania regional headquarters at the campus.

By combining Classiq ’s software engineering platform and education with FreeYa Mind Campus’s quantum infrastructure, the partnership strengthens the Romanian and wider European quantum ecosystems, developing the skills, workflows and applications needed to put that infrastructure to effective use.

Building on the success of FreeYa Mind Campus, we are bringing those elements together, and Classiq will provide the scalable software foundation that lets universities, enterprises and public institutions develop quantum applications,” said Regev Yativ , CRO at Classiq.

TAIYI Quantum reported integrating its first prototype within six months, developing real-time feedback with latency in the tens of microseconds and releasing LUOSHU, an open-source compiler for neutral-atom hardware.

PRESS RELEASE — TAIYI Quantum, a quantum computing company developing ytterbium (Yb) neutral-atom technology, announced that its cumulative funding has exceeded RMB 1 billion (approximately US$140 million) following its latest financing round, less than a year after its founding in January 2026.
The latest round attracted participation from venture capital firms, strategic investors, and institutional funds, bringing the company’s cumulative financing to more than RMB 1 billion.

The funding will support the company’s development of scalable neutral-atom quantum computing systems, with a particular focus on quantum error correction, fault-tolerant architectures, real-time control, and hardware–software integration.
“Quantum computing is fundamentally a long-term systems engineering challenge,” said Zhenghao Fang, Co-founder and CEO of TAIYI Quantum.

“Our priority is to translate investment into engineering capabilities, bring together exceptional talent, and build the technological foundations for practical quantum computing.” Building a Quantum Computing Architecture Around Fault Tolerance TAIYI Quantum is pursuing an ytterbium-based neutral-atom architecture designed with fault-tolerant quantum computing as its long-term objective.

While neutral-atom platforms offer promising scalability and flexible qubit connectivity, translating physical qubits into reliable logical operations requires advances across quantum error correction, measurement, real-time feedback, and system architecture.
Together, these developments reflect TAIYI Quantum’s focus on integrating hardware, control, and software capabilities required for future fault-tolerant quantum computing systems.

items.originalTitle: Anduril awarded contract to expand US Army’s next-gen battlefield command system
items.summary: The Army awarded Anduril Industries a contract on Sept. 30 worth up to $1.8 billion over five years to help the service transition its new battlefield software from the experimentation phase to the fielding phase. Anduril previously helped develop the prototype for the service’s Next Generation Command and Control, or NGC2, for the 4th Infantry Division, using its proprietary AI-powered operating system Lattice.

evidenceRecords.text: The Army awarded Anduril Industries a contract on Sept. 30 worth up to $1.8 billion over five years to help the service transition its new battlefield software from the experimentation phase to the fielding phase.

Anduril previously helped develop the prototype for the service’s Next Generation Command and Control, or NGC2, for the 4th Infantry Division, using its proprietary AI-powered operating system Lattice.

“A common data layer allows the Army to integrate new systems without rebuilding the underlying architecture for every sensor, application, or weapon, so new capabilities can be fielded on the same foundation as those already in use,” Anduril said.

The Army awarded $162.8 million to Anduril to continue working on NGC2’s common data baseline, or software foundation, as it begins to implement it across the service’s I Corps, which commands service members across the Indo-Pacific.
The contract contains options that can grow its value up to $1.8 billion.
Anduril, along with Palantir, Raft and Striveworks, have helped build out the baseline.
The NGC2 system will allow technologies, weapons, sensors, devices and applications from across the force to operate on the same network and increase decision-making speed on the battlefield.

By expanding the NGC2 system to the I Corps, technologies will have to figure out ways to connect to the same network despite being separated by thousands of miles and experiencing interrupted or degraded connectivity.
This will provide the Army and Anduril an opportunity to test how well information flows between the systems as they access the NGC2 framework in a myriad of environments.

During a July 2026 ten-day event at Fort Irwin, California, entitled Project Convergence-Capstone 6 , the Army asked 10,000 participants from U.S. and allied forces, as well as industry partners using 90 technologies to test software for the NGC2.
Afterward, the Army awarded a contract to Anduril to develop the software prototype for NGC2 for the 4th Infantry Division.
Over the past year, Anduril has conducted several operational exercises in collaboration with the Army to test the NGC2’s common data layer baseline.

items.originalTitle: US Army to stand up command for unmanned and autonomous warfare
items.summary: The U.S. Army has ordered the creation of its own command for autonomous systems, a day after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced a new four-star military command for unmanned and autonomous warfare. An Oct. 1 memo signed by Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle directs the Army vice chief of staff to establish the U.S. Army Futures and Autonomous Systems Command, or FASCOM. It also tells the assistant secretary of the Army for acquisition, logistics and technology, who oversees how the Army buys weapons, to put one office in charge of purchasing its priority autonomous systems.

evidenceRecords.text: The U.S. Army has ordered the creation of its own command for autonomous systems, a day after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced a new four-star military command for unmanned and autonomous warfare.
An Oct. 1 memo signed by Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle directs the Army vice chief of staff to establish the U.S. Army Futures and Autonomous Systems Command, or FASCOM.

It also tells the assistant secretary of the Army for acquisition, logistics and technology, who oversees how the Army buys weapons, to put one office in charge of purchasing its priority autonomous systems.
Telle wrote that he issued the memo under guidance from Hegseth’s Sept. 30 State of the Force address .
The memo does not say who will lead FASCOM, where it will be based or when it will be established.
“Specifics on structure, command, mission, etc. will be announced at a future date,” Col.
Marty Meiners, an Army spokesperson, told Defense News.
The new acquisition office, a Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Autonomy, would have single authority over buying the Army’s priority autonomous systems.

“We are forging the U.S. Army Futures and Autonomous Systems Command to get cutting-edge technology into the hands of soldiers, while prioritizing autonomy in our formations, our acquisitions, and our training to dominate the future of warfare.” Hegseth announced the Autonomous Warfare Command, or AutoWarCom, during his Sept. 30 State of the Force address at Marine Corps Base Quantico, Virginia, Military Times reported .

Hegseth’s own memo, “ Project Agincourt: Pathway to the Autonomous Warfare Command ,” signed the same day as his address, puts the Pentagon’s unmanned systems office in charge of Project Agincourt, an effort to lay the groundwork for AutoWarCom.

The terminals, which are distributed and managed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX, are a key component of Ukraine’s military operations and the sudden restrictions on the terminals travelling at high speeds on Tuesday evening led to the failure of several combat missions, said an adviser on military technology to Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

Ukrainian soldiers in combat have suddenly had their access to Starlink satellite internet terminals restricted as the Trump administration has increased pressure on Ukraine to halt long-range strikes on Russia’s oil industry immediately.
The sudden outage came as Russia launched ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US for a second night.
For years, the US has provided Ukraine with intelligence when strikes were about to take place.
Donald Trump has denied that his administration has cut intelligence sharing with Ukraine.

Zelenskyy also indicated that the US was continuing to share intelligence with Ukraine in an interview with NPR aired on Wednesday, but confirmed that military advisers had received threats from the US that intelligence sharing could be limited.
Ukraine did not receive any warning before Russia launched its first barrage of ballistic missiles on Tuesday evening, according to Col Yurii Ihnat, a spokesperson for the air force.
But it did receive warnings from “foreign partners” about three subsequent barrages, leaving further confusion about whether or not the US is intentionally withholding intelligence from Ukraine.

Limiting Starlink’s access speeds would have a significant effect on Ukraine’s mid-range strike campaign, where it uses the satellite internet system to navigate drones to hit targets behind the front in Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine.
But there have been no reports that access for static Starlink terminals have been cut, meaning critical battlefield communications for soldiers should remain unaffected.
The detection of incoming Russian missiles and drones relies on other technologies.
Musk, an ally of Trump, had previously cut off Starlink service to Ukrainian soldiers during an offensive that took a small amount of Russian territory.

evidenceRecords.text: Despite massive technological shifts, that paradigm still holds, which is why the U.S. Army and Navy have teamed up to keep systems operational — even in the extreme cold of the Arctic .

The team focused on different configurations of thermal wrappings, insulation and other components to ensure that parts of the kit’s components that are particularly vulnerable to cracking and freezing — hoses, valves, bladders and pumps — were able to withstand the greater threshold for cold, according to a recent Army release.

“Our armed forces live and operate in extremely cold and difficult conditions, so having these facilities operational is important for their physical and mental health while serving in the Arctic and other high-north environments,” said Dr. Dan Tague, a research chemist at CRREL, one of seven U.S. Army Engineer Research and Development Center laboratories.
Despite massive technological shifts, that paradigm still holds, which is why the U.S. Army and Navy have teamed up to keep systems operational — even in the extreme cold of the Arctic.
As the Department of Defense eyes greater operability in the far north, these low temperatures can wreak havoc on equipment and machinery (and toilets), with ice becoming enemy No. 1.

Which is why the Naval Facilities Engineering and Expeditionary Warfare Center, or NAVFAC EXWC, and the Cold Regions Research and Engineering Laboratory, or CRREL, began working with both branches to field a rapidly deployable Triple Container rigid-wall shelter system usable in temperatures as low as -50 degrees Fahrenheit.
The already fielded version can operate in temperatures as low as -15 degrees Fahrenheit.
The result, per the release, far exceeded the objectives, with the TRICON-based system staying operational down to -65 degrees Fahrenheit.
Testing took place in CRREL’s New Hampshire-based Extreme Cold Chamber, a 288-square-foot cold room capable of reaching temperatures as low as -90 degrees Fahrenheit, per the release.

While military units typically have to wait until the Alaskan winter reaches its peak to simulate similar conditions, the controlled environment allowed the research team to create conditions similar to those of the real world.

The test, or Neurocognitive Assessment Tool, is computer-based and records neurological activity, such as attention, concentration, reaction time, memory, processing speed and decision-making.
Testing started in 2024 in response to reports about the effects that routine weapons training can have on the brain, including traumatic brain injury.

Active-duty, National Guard and Reserve soldiers in high-risk military occupational specialties, including combat engineers and explosive ordnance technicians, as well as troops operating heavy weapons systems, must take the assessment every year, starting soon after they enlist.
All other soldiers are required to test every three years.
Medical professionals use the data to monitor service members’ cognitive health throughout their military careers, allowing them to spot significant changes, including potential brain injuries.

“[The NCAT] is an important part of taking care of soldiers, but what this does is, it sets a baseline for reaction times and for memory,” Jordan Gillis, assistant secretary of the Army for installations, energy and environment, said in a release.

“By establishing a baseline for all soldiers, we’re able to monitor brain health, as well as … let medical providers help with treatment, if required.” According to the Sept. 30 release, the Army is expected to publish a directive about the Neurocognitive Assessment Tool and a broader overpressure program, which includes hazard assessment, exposure tracking, risk mitigation, cognitive monitoring, information management, illness and injury reporting and training and education.
“The takeaway is we are trying to take care of soldiers and monitor their health,” Gillis said.

“And if there is an impact, we’ll be able to treat them.” Reaching the milestone of 97% of soldiers being tested on the NCAT “demonstrates our commitment to cognitive safety, medical readiness and warfighting capability,” Gillis added.

The announcement of the milestone came just one month after the Government Accountability Office released the findings of its investigation into the ability of military services to provide the baseline cognitive assessments.

evidenceRecords.text: Artificial neural networks can learn to recognize images, use language, or write computer code.
Like the brain’s circuits, they reorganize themselves as they learn, adjusting the strengths of their connections to improve their performance.

Lisa Yang Integrative Computational Neuroscience (ICoN) Center argue that a crucial metric for the biological plausibility of an artificial neural network’s approach to learning is the network’s ability to organize itself, without the guiding hand of a developer.
They show that it is possible for an artificial neural network to build its own learning machinery.

“That’s not achievable by just designing a circuit that works very well.” An artificial neural network’s value to neuroscience should instead be judged by the extent to which it can organize itself — not just its connections, but also the machinery that adjusts those connections.

“If the synaptic motifs we propose are, in fact, used by the brain to do what backpropagation does for artificial neural networks, then we will have a strong connection at the level of fundamental mechanisms between artificial and natural networks — between machines and brains,” he says.

As robots move beyond warehouses and other controlled environments and into everyday life, solving these navigation challenges will be critical to achieving broad consumer acceptance and large-scale deployment.

At RoboBusiness 2026, Aaron Edsinger, the co-founder and CEO of Hello Robot , and Matt Anderson, the co-founder and CEO of A&K Robotics , will take part in the session, “Shared Spaces: Navigating Challenges for Indoor Robots.” RoboBusiness will be on Oct. 20 and 21 in Santa Clara, Calif.

With a passion for building robots and robot companies, he has founded four companies focused on bringing human collaborative robots to the consumer, manufacturing, healthcare and research markets.

As robotics director at Google, Edsinger led the business, product and technical development of two of Google’s central investments in robotics, and worked closely with senior vice president and C-level executives to define the overall robotics strategy.
Edsinger is a recognized robotics innovator with a broad understanding of the entire robot product design stack, including human–robot interaction, UX design, and mechanical design.
Matt Anderson is co-founder and CEO of A&K Robotics, which is building autonomous mobility infrastructure for complex, human-centered environments such as airports.

He leads the company’s product strategy, which includes Cruz, a self-driving mobility robot that carries passengers through high-traffic, dynamic environments such as airport terminals, and Kineos AI, a platform for socially intelligent autonomy that enables systems to move naturally through dynamic spaces.
Anderson brings credibility with enterprise and public-sector partners by translating advanced autonomy into institution-ready solutions.

Engineers and technicians on Aug. 31, 2026, used a crane to position the spacecraft within the towering chamber, where Griffin-1 alternately baked at up to 167 degrees Fahrenheit (75 degrees Celsius) and froze at temperatures as low as minus 148 F (minus 100 C).
Figure A In Figure A, engineers and technicians move Griffin-1 through a hallway leading to the 25-Foot Space Simulator on Aug. 31.

Figure B Figure B shows Griffin-1 on July 29 in an anechoic chamber for electromagnetic interference and electromagnetic compatibility testing, which ensures signals from the spacecraft’s electronic components don’t interfere with one another.

Figure C In Figure C, taken on July 20, Griffin-1 rotates rapidly on a special table to measure its mass properties, enabling engineers to look for any unexpected wobbles as they assess how the vehicle will move through space — vital information for determining the spacecraft’s readiness for flight and surface operations.

Figure D In Figure D, microphones are arrayed around Griffin-1 on Aug. 12 during acoustic testing in which giant horns powered by compressed gaseous nitrogen blast the spacecraft with up to 153 decibels inside the sealed acoustic chamber to mimic the roar of launch.

Griffin-1 also endured vibration testing, during which hundreds of sensors monitored the spacecraft as a “shaker table” rattled it in three directions — with increasingly intense force — to simulate the ride out of Earth’s atmosphere atop a rocket.
After proving its mettle at JPL, Griffin-1 was shipped back across the country to Voyager Lunar Systems’ Pittsburgh facility for final assembly.
Part of NASA’s CLPS (Commercial Lunar Payload Services) initiative within the Moon Base Program, Griffin-1 is expected to launch in late 2026 aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket.
